title: The order outbox, the poll endpoint, the seed script and the README quickstart

events.text: The order outbox, the poll endpoint, the seed script and the README quickstart
events.body:
## Goal
Turn an approval into exactly one order for the merchant side — an outbox row written in the
approving transaction, a cursor-based poll, an acknowledgement that moves the requisition to
`ordered` — and make the whole v1 flow runnable from a clean clone in three commands.

## Context
Part of #6.
Builds on split 3: the approve path, the transaction helper, `writeAudit`, the idempotency
machinery and the typed refusals already exist. This split adds the row at the end of that
transaction and the two endpoints that drain it.

Honor D-011 (`order_outbox` with `id` (monotonic INTEGER cursor), `org_id`, `requisition_id`,
`payload_json`, `created_at`, `delivered_at`, `ack_by`; the row is written **in the approving
transaction**; `GET /api/v1/outbox?after=<id>&limit=n` with a merchant-scoped token;
`POST /api/v1/outbox/ack {through_id}` moves the requisition to `ordered` and stamps `delivered_at`;
delivery is **at-least-once** and the merchant dedups on `id`; **no webhook** — G-006 holds the
trigger), D-009 (`ordered` is set here and only here; `approved → ordered` is the only edge into it),
D-007 (the ack writes an audit line per requisition it orders), D-010 (the ack is idempotent: the
cursor only moves forward, and a replayed ack is a no-op returning the same response), D-004 (the
outbox is scoped like everything else — a merchant token for org B never sees org A's rows), D-003
(the payload carries integer minor units and the currency, and the total is recomputed from the
lines at payload build time, not copied from a cache), D-017 (the cursor is an integer *because* it
must be ordered; business ids stay random), D-018 (the seed script reads `.env`, the service never
does; the script prints tokens to stdout once and never writes them to a file in the repo).

**Do NOT**: emit a webhook, add a retry/backoff engine, or introduce a queue; mark `ordered` at
approval time; delete outbox rows on ack (stamp them — the feed stays replayable); let the ack move
the cursor backwards; build the payload from anything other than the requisition's own lines; commit
a `.env`, a token, or a database file; make the seed script bypass the `OrgScope` repositories.

The seed script (`npm run seed`) creates: two organisations (one EUR, one JPY — the exponent-0 case
must exist in the demo), a handful of catalogue items each, cost centres with owners, a buyer, an
approver, a finance approver and a merchant integration per org, and a three-row rule table per org
(`self` up to a small amount, `cost_centre_owner` up to a larger one, `finance` unbounded — the
terminal row D-008 requires). It prints the minted tokens and the URLs to open.

New rows: none reserved. An addendum to D-011 is expected if the payload shape needs fields this
issue did not name.

## Acceptance criteria
- [ ] Approving writes exactly one `order_outbox` row in the same transaction; a fault injected
      after the state change and before commit leaves **no** row, no audit line and no state change
      (one test proves all three together).
- [ ] `GET /api/v1/outbox?after=0` returns rows in `id` order; `after=<last id>` returns the
      remainder; `limit` is honoured and capped; an empty feed returns an empty list, not an error.
- [ ] A requisition never appears twice in one drain, and re-polling from an older cursor returns
      the same rows with the same payloads (replayable).
- [ ] `POST /api/v1/outbox/ack {through_id}` moves every acknowledged requisition to `ordered`,
      stamps `delivered_at` and `ack_by`, and writes one audit line each; a second identical ack is a
      no-op with the same response; a `through_id` lower than the current cursor is a no-op, not an
      error; a `through_id` the caller never received is `validation_failed`.
- [ ] A merchant token for org B polling or acking against org A's rows sees nothing and changes
      nothing — asserted in the cross-org leak suite.
- [ ] A buyer or approver token cannot call either outbox endpoint (`not_authorised`).
- [ ] The payload's total equals the sum of the line totals recomputed at build time, carries the
      currency, and a JPY requisition renders exponent 0 correctly end to end.
- [ ] `npm run seed` is idempotent (a second run does not duplicate organisations) and works
      offline against a fresh database file.
- [ ] The README quickstart works verbatim on a clean clone with no network beyond `npm ci`:
      install, seed, start, then the full walkthrough — draft → submit → reject with a reason → copy
      forward → approve → poll → ack → `ordered` — with the exact commands and the URLs to open.
      A test executes the API half of that walkthrough end to end.
- [ ] The board is green; still no runtime dependency.

## Test expectations
`node --test`, in-process, `:memory:` for unit tests and a temp-file database for the seed and
quickstart tests (cleaned up afterwards). Suites: `outbox/transactional` (including the fault
injection), `outbox/cursor` (ordering, limits, replay, backwards ack), `outbox/tenancy` (extends the
mandatory cross-org leak suite), `seed/idempotent`, `flow/end-to-end` (the README walkthrough as
code — the Arc 1 exit criterion expressed as a test). No network, no listening port except the one
integration test that binds `127.0.0.1:0`.

## Out of scope
Webhooks and any push delivery (G-006); retries, backoff, dead-lettering; a real commerce backend or
any external call; the merchant-side agent (G-009); a merchant UI; Docker images and deployment;
rate limiting (G-010); the buyer drafting agent (Arc 2).

Depends on: #3

The order outbox, the merchant poll and ack, the seed script and the README quickstart
events.body:
Closes #5

## Summary
Approval now writes exactly one `order_outbox` row **in the approving transaction** (D-011), so
an order can neither be lost nor emitted for a change that rolled back — `recordApproval` is
still the one place `approved` is written, and the row goes in there. Two merchant routes drain
it: `GET /api/v1/outbox?after=&limit=` over the monotonic integer cursor (D-017), and
`POST /api/v1/outbox/ack {through_id}`, which is the **only** path into `ordered` (D-009) and
writes one audit line per requisition it orders (D-007). Acknowledged rows are stamped, never
deleted, so an older cursor replays the same rows with the same payload bytes — at-least-once,
merchant dedups on `id`. No webhook, no retries, no queue (G-006 still holds the trigger).

Authority is a fifth role, `merchant`, added by migration `0003` (the `person_roles` CHECK is
rebuilt the way `0002` rebuilt the key ledger). It is a role on a person row rather than a
second credential format because D-005 knows one token shape, roles are read live (D-006), and
`order_outbox.ack_by` has to be able to name who acknowledged. A buyer or approver token is
`not_authorised` on both routes; the organisation comes from the scope, so a merchant token of
org B reads and stamps nothing of org A (D-004).

`npm run seed` builds the two-organisation demo (Acme GmbH / EUR, Kabuki KK / JPY) the README
quickstart walks through — through the `OrgScope` repositories only, idempotent, tokens printed
once and written to no file (D-018). The README gains the three-command quickstart and the full
walkthrough; `test/flow/end-to-end.test.ts` executes its API half, so a wrong README is a red
board.

## Evidence for the reviewers
**Board, green, on this branch:** `npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run lint &&
check-anchors.mjs && render.mjs --check` — **434 tests, 0 fail** (402 before), lint clean,
`anchors: 24 D · 19 G · 10 M rows, every reference resolves`, `framework: 19 generated files
match`. Still zero runtime dependencies. New suites: `outbox/transactional` (6),
`outbox/cursor` (13), `outbox/tenancy` (3), `seed/idempotent` (4), `flow/end-to-end` (2), plus
2 appended rows and 2 appended write cases in the mandatory cross-org leak suite (now 31 tests)
— both mandatory suites (leak, lifecycle/authority) green.

**Mutations — eight tried, and what each one did:**

| # | Mutation | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | drop the `outbox.append` from `recordApproval` | 🔴 12 tests across all three outbox suites |
| 2 | `selectAfter` no longer binds `org_id` | 🔴 3 — `outbox.listAfter` leak case + both HTTP tenancy cases |
| 3 | acknowledged rows **deleted** instead of stamped | 🔴 4 — replay, ack, fresh-ack no-op, backwards ack |
| 4 | remove the `through_id > maxId()` guard | 🔴 2 — `validation_failed` case **and** the cross-org ack case |
| 5 | merchant guard → "any identified person" | 🔴 1 — the buyer/approver authority case |
| 6 | payload total = first line instead of the sum | **survived at first** — every payload assertion used a single-line requisition, so "sum" and "first line" were indistinguishable. Closed with a hand-derived three-line case (3×129 900 + 2×29 900 + 1×8 900 = 458 400); the mutation is now 🔴 |
| 7 | seed always creates, never re-finds | 🔴 1 — the second-run case |
| 8 | ack hard-codes `'ordered'` instead of asking `decide` | **survived at first** — no public path can put an unapproved requisition in the outbox, so the check could not produce its case. Closed by producing it at the repository seam (an order row for a draft): the ack must throw and roll back, never quietly order a draft. Now 🔴 |

Both survivors are in the commit `fc109f3`; they are the reason the suite count moved from 432
to 434.

**One design change came out of the measurement, not the spec.** The first version of the ack
scanned every row up to `through_id` and returned every requisition the cursor covered — p95
1.85 ms at 300 orders and rising with the history, plus a response body that grows forever. The
work window is now `cursor < id ≤ through_id` and undelivered (p95 0.29 ms at 1 000 orders,
flat), and `ordered` lists what *this call* moved.

**Deviation from the issue, stated plainly.** The criterion "a second identical ack is a no-op
with the same response" is met in two pieces rather than one: a genuine retry carries the same
`Idempotency-Key` and is answered with the first call's bytes (D-010, `Idempotent-Replayed:
true`), and a *fresh* ack of an already acknowledged cursor stamps nothing, orders nothing and
answers `ordered: []` with the cursor unchanged. Making the response literally identical without
the key would have required the unbounded scan and response above. Both halves have their own
test. The D-011 addendum says this in the row.

Other notes: no `🏛 Design` comment existed (size:M, no architect stage). Nothing under
`src/web/` was created or touched; the router change is one import plus one spread in
`ROUTES`; `recordApproval` gained one call; the README edits are additive sections.

## Docs
- **D-011 · addendum #5** — who polls (the `merchant` token), the payload shape
  (`version`/`totalMinor` recomputed from the lines/`lines[]`) and `ORDER_PAYLOAD_VERSION`, the
  two routes' answers, the `limit` cap, the ack's work window and the two-piece idempotence,
  and the rule that a refusal *after* the state change throws.
- **D-006 · addendum #5** — the fifth role, `merchant`; what it grants and what it does not.
- **D-009 · addendum #5** — the `approved → order → ordered` row is live, with its only caller.
- **M-004** — measured: our own side of the handoff, approve 0.297 ms p50 / 0.380 ms p95 and ack
  0.232 / 0.291 over n=1 000, in-process, one run, on the implementer's MacBook. Explicitly
  **not** measured and still pending: the poll interval sweep, a real socket round trip, any
  concurrency. It also records the scan the measurement caught.
- **README** — the quickstart (install, seed, start + the nine-step walkthrough), the two new
  routes in the API table, and the order-handoff paragraph.
- No new `G-` row: nothing here opened a question the existing rows do not already hold
  (G-006 webhook, G-010 rate limits).

## Dependencies
None. `package.json` gains one script (`seed`); `devDependencies` are unchanged, three names.

## Audit contribution
Two, both inside the transaction that changed the state. The existing `approve` line is
unchanged and now commits together with the order row. The acknowledgement writes one `order`
line per requisition it moves: organisation from the scope, actor the merchant person behind the
token, `from_state: approved`, `to_state: ordered`, the stored `rule_id`, and the total
recomputed from the lines with its currency. A refused line throws and rolls the whole
acknowledgement back.

## Manual steps
None that a machine cannot do — but the README quickstart is the thing a human should read
once against a real terminal. `npm run seed && npm start` and the nine curl steps were run by
hand on this branch (the seed's output shape, including the cost-centre id the walkthrough needs,
came from that run); the API half of the same walkthrough is `test/flow/end-to-end.test.ts`.

## Fix round 1 (#5 review) — evidence

Board on `97abb2b`, in a clean worktree: `npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm test &&
npm run lint && check-anchors && render --check` → **474 pass, 0 fail**, lint clean,
`anchors: 25 D · 23 G · 10 M rows, every reference resolves`, `framework: 19 generated
files match`. Eight new cases (466 → 474).

**The quickstart, run verbatim from a clean clone** (`git clone` of this branch into a temp
directory, `data/` and `.env` local to it): `npm ci` → the README's `printf … > .env` →
`npm run seed` → `npm start`, which built and then logged
`ready … "port":3123,"migrationsApplied":[]` with **no exported variables** — only the `.env`
the quickstart writes. The nine curl steps then ran green: draft `201`
(`total 259800 EUR`) · submit `200 submitted` · reject `200` · copy `201` · submit `200` ·
approve `200` · poll → one item, `nextAfter: 1`, `cursor: 0`, `payload.version: 2` with **no
`ruleId`/`ruleCode`** · ack → `{"throughId":1,"cursor":1,"ordered":["…"]}` · detail →
`ordered`, history `draft.copied · submit · approve · order`. The same merchant token then
got `403 not_authorised` on `/requisitions`, `/requisitions/:id` and `/rules`. `SIGTERM`
logged `stopped`. *(The only deviation: `PORT=3123` went into that same `.env`, because port
3000 on this machine is held by an unrelated Docker process.)*

**Mutations tried this round, each red:**
- `nextAfter: last.id` → `nextAfter: after` — `test/outbox/cursor.test.ts` 1 fail (the new
  paging case; it was 434/434 green before).
- `audienceGuard` neutralised in `dispatch` — `test/http/authority.test.ts` 1 fail (the
  refusal's wording pins *which* seam answered).
- `start` back to `node dist/main.js` with `dist/` removed — `test/flow/quickstart.test.ts`
  1 fail, `the service exited with 1`. That is the 🔴 the old board could not see.
- Removing the merchant narrowing also turns three pre-existing cases red, which is the
  intended behaviour change: `any member of the organisation may read any requisition` now
  names the four human roles explicitly.

**Docs this round:** `docs/08-security.md` (Actors → Merchant, and T9), D-006 addendum
(enforcement + separation of duties), D-011 addendum (e) (what the payload does not carry,
`version` 2), G-022 (merchant + approver), G-023 (the instance-wide outbox cursor),
`docs/13-roadmap.md` (the Arc 1 exit criterion now names the secret and the build).

**Deviation:** the order payload's `version` went `1` → `2` rather than staying `1`. Nothing
consumes it yet, and that field exists precisely so a shape change is visible.

## 🔐 Security review

Branch `feat/issue-5`, worktree at `origin/feat/issue-5` (`fc109f3`). PR evidence reused:
`npm ci && npm test` → **434 pass, 0 fail** on this branch. Two probes of my own, both below.

What I checked and found sound, so it is not repeated as a finding: every `order_outbox`
statement binds `scope.orgId` first (`listAfter`, `listPending`, `selectById`, `selectMaxId`,
`selectCursor`, `stampDelivered`, and `append` re-checks the requisition against the scope),
so a merchant token of org B reads and stamps nothing of org A; `through_id > maxId()` is
`validation_failed` against the **org's own** max, so a global id belonging to another tenant
is refused, and a `through_id` at or below the cursor opens an empty window rather than an
error; the `limit` is capped twice (service `Math.min(limit, MAX_POLL_LIMIT)` and again in
`listAfter`) and `limit=0`/non-decimal are refused at the route; the ack's audit line names
the merchant person behind the token (`scope.actor.personId`) with the stored `rule_id` and a
total recomputed from the lines, and every refusal after the state change throws so the
transaction rolls back; the ack is a mutating route, so it goes through the
`Idempotency-Key` + `(org, actor, endpoint, key)` ledger like every other write.

**Probe 1 — migration `0003`.** Applied `0001`+`0002` to a fresh database, inserted an org, a
person and two roles (`buyer`, `admin`), then ran `0003`: both rows carried over byte for
byte, `PRAGMA foreign_key_check` empty, `PRAGMA integrity_check` `ok`, the rebuilt `CHECK`
carries the five roles and still refuses a sixth, the `person_id` foreign key still fires on a
dangling id, and `person_roles_by_org` is back. Clean — **no finding**.

**Probe 2 — a merchant-only token off the outbox routes.** See 🔴 below.

### 🔴 Findings

**1 · A merchant-only token reads the whole organisation, not just the order feed.**
`merchantGuard` correctly fences `GET /outbox` and `POST /outbox/ack`, but this PR introduces
a new principal — an *external* service credential, held by the merchant — and the existing
read routes have no role check at all: `detail`, `list` (`src/app/requisitions.ts:829`, `:837`)
and `ruleTable` (`:905`) gate on organisation membership only.

Probe, in-process against `dispatch` with the branch's own fixture: a buyer creates a draft
that is never submitted, never approved and never in the outbox; then, with a token for the
`merchant`-only person:

```
MERCHANT GET /api/v1/requisitions            -> 200  {"items":[{... "state":"draft" ...}]}
MERCHANT GET /api/v1/requisitions/<draft id> -> 200  full detail, lines and amounts
MERCHANT GET /api/v1/rules                   -> 200  seq 10 ≤ 10000 self · seq 20 ≤ 500000
                                                     cost_centre_owner · seq 30 finance
```

So the merchant integration reads drafts, rejected and cancelled requisitions, their line
descriptions, quantities and amounts, rejection reasons, and the organisation's whole approval
ladder with its thresholds — the last of which is exactly the data an external counterparty
would use to size orders just under an approval threshold.

This contradicts the threat model this PR is reviewed against. `docs/08-security.md`, the
Actors table, gives **Merchant integration** the reach "the outbox feed and its
acknowledgement (D-011)" and the note "reads approved requisitions; writes nothing but acks".
T9 says "The outbox endpoint is scoped like everything else" — which is true and is not the
hole; the hole is everything that is *not* the outbox endpoint. The `merchant` role is
additive on `person_roles`, so today's shared-queue design (any member sees the queue, which
is deliberate for buyers) silently hands an outside party the same view.

The fix is a narrowing, not a redesign: either the read routes require one of the *human*
roles (`buyer`/`approver`/`finance`/`admin`) and a `merchant`-only scope is `not_authorised`
there, or `merchant` is made exclusive of the other four at the grant seam. Either way
`docs/08-security.md`'s Merchant row and the D-006 addendum should then state the reach they
actually have, and the lifecycle/authority suite should pin a merchant-only token getting
`not_authorised` on `GET /api/v1/requisitions`, `/requisitions/:id` and `/rules`.

### 🟡 Nits

**1 · The outbox cursor is an instance-wide sequence, so it leaks other tenants' order
volume.** `order_outbox.id` is `INTEGER PRIMARY KEY AUTOINCREMENT` over one table for every
organisation (`0001_initial.ts:155`), and this PR is what first hands that id to an outside
party as `OutboxItemView.id`/`nextAfter`. The gap between two consecutive ids in *my own* feed
is the number of approvals every other organisation on the instance committed in between — a
merchant can meter the whole instance, and a competitor's merchant token can meter it too.
D-017 makes business ids random rather than sequential for precisely this reason, and
`docs/08-security.md` lists "the existence … of another organisation" as asset 3. Content is
not exposed and the ordering guarantee the design rests on is per-org monotonicity, which a
per-org sequence would also give, so this is hardening rather than a block — but it belongs in
a `G-` row with the trigger "the first instance that serves two organisations with competing
merchants" if it is not fixed here.

**2 · The order payload hands the merchant the approval rule that cleared it.**
`orderPayload` includes `ruleId` and `ruleCode` (`src/domain/order.ts:41-42`) plus
`buyerPersonId` and `costCentreId`. The merchant needs the lines, the total, the currency and
the requisition number to fulfil an order; which internal approval rule matched is internal
control data. `buyerPersonId`/`costCentreId` are opaque UUIDs and carry no name or email, so
they are defensible as correlation handles — the rule pair is not. (With 🔴 1 fixed this
becomes the *only* way the ladder reaches the merchant, so it is worth dropping in the same
change; `version` already exists to make the shape change detectable.)

**3 · An unscoped cross-instance lookup is now on the public surface.**
`instanceFindOrgByName` (`src/db/instance.ts`) queries `orgs` with no `OrgScope` and is
exported from `src/index.ts`. The doc comment says "never a request path", and the seed's use
is legitimate housekeeping — but a comment is the only thing standing between it and a future
handler, and `name` is not unique, so "the first match by creation order" is a silent
tie-break across tenants. Consider keeping it un-exported from the package index, or naming it
so the seam is unmissable (`instanceFindOrgByNameUnscoped`).

**4 · Nothing stops one person holding `merchant` and `approver`.** `grantRole` takes any of
the five, so an admin can give the approver of a cost centre the merchant role as well; that
person could then approve a requisition and acknowledge its own order, and both audit lines
would name them — honest, but no separation of duties. Worth one sentence in the D-006
addendum saying whether that combination is allowed, or a grant-time refusal.

VERDICT: findings (1 red, 4 nits)

## 🧪 Quality review

Board reproduced on `feat/issue-5`: `npm ci && npm run typecheck && npm test && npm run lint`
green — **434 tests, 0 fail**, lint clean, `anchors: 24 D · 19 G · 10 M rows, every reference
resolves`. Two mutations of my own, both of which the PR's eight did not try; both survived
(below). The outbox row inside `recordApproval`'s transaction, the cursor window
`cursor < id ≤ through_id`, the merchant guard, the tenancy binding, migration `0003`, the seed's
`OrgScope`-only writes and stdout-only tokens, and the D-006/D-009/D-011 addenda plus M-004's
honest "half measured, half pending" all hold up. The flagged deviation on the fresh second ack
is fine: `cursor` still tells the merchant the truth and the D-011 addendum states it plainly.

The red findings are both in the quickstart.

### 🔴 Must fix

**1 · The README quickstart does not run verbatim — the acceptance criterion it answers.**
`README.md:56-64` tells a clean clone to run `npm ci` → write `.env` → `npm run seed` → `npm start`.
`package.json:16` is `"start": "node … dist/main.js"`, with **no build step and no
`--env-file-if-exists=.env`**. Both halves fail, verified in this worktree:

- `dist/` is gitignored, and nothing in the quickstart builds it:
  `npm start` → `Error: Cannot find module '…/dist/main.js'`, `code: 'MODULE_NOT_FOUND'`.
- after `npm run build`, with the `.env` the quickstart just wrote and the variable not exported:
  `npm start` → `configuration error: REQUISIT_TOKEN_SECRET is required`.

That is the documented behaviour, not a bug in `main.ts`: `README.md:45-46` says `.env` is
"gitignored and never read by the service itself", and `mint-token`/`seed` are the two scripts
that pass `--env-file-if-exists`. So the quickstart contradicts its own README two sections
above, and a reader gets to step 1 of the walkthrough with no server. The fix is in the
quickstart block (add the build, and source/export the secret — or give `start` the same
`--env-file-if-exists=.env` the other two scripts have). `scripts/seed.ts:302` prints the same
instruction (`Start the service with \`npm start\``) and has to move with it.

**2 · `README.md:131-133` makes a claim the change cannot keep.**
> `test/flow/end-to-end.test.ts` executes this same walkthrough against a seeded database, so
> if the walkthrough is wrong, the board is red.

`test/flow/end-to-end.test.ts:31-53` opens a temp database, calls `seed()` in process and drives
`dispatch` directly. It never runs `npm ci`, never writes `.env`, never runs `npm run seed` as a
process and never starts a server — i.e. it cannot see exactly the four lines that are broken in
finding 1, which is how they reached review with a green board. This is the "a check that cannot
produce the case" shape from the standards, stated in the tree as a guarantee. Either narrow the
sentence to the API half (as the PR body honestly does) or extend the suite to spawn
`npm run seed` and `npm start` against a temp `REQUISIT_DB_PATH`.

### 🟡 Nits

1. **`nextAfter` is unpinned.** Mutating `src/app/outbox.ts:125` to `nextAfter: after` — the
   paging cursor never advances, so a merchant driving its loop off it pages forever — leaves
   **434/434 green**. The only assertion on the field in the tree is the empty-feed
   `nextAfter === 0` at `test/outbox/cursor.test.ts:101`: an absence assertion with no companion
   presence assertion in the same run. `the feed comes back in id order…` (line 104) gets its
   `after=` values from the items, not from `nextAfter`. D-011 addendum (c) and `README.md:117`
   both document the field; one assertion that the next poll's `after` came from the previous
   answer closes it.
2. **`delivered_at IS NULL` in `selectPending` (`src/db/repos/outbox.ts:84`) is decoration.**
   Removing it also leaves **434/434 green**. It is genuinely redundant given the invariant the
   comment above it states (every row at or below the cursor is delivered, ids are
   `AUTOINCREMENT`) — so either drop it, or pin the invariant with a case that would notice if a
   future change broke it.
3. **Migration `0003`'s carry-over claim has no case.** The file says "Every existing row is

## 🔐 Security review — re-review after fix round 1 (97abb2b)

Scope: the fix at its seams, new reds only. Worktree on `origin/feat/issue-5`, `npm ci && npm test` → **474 pass, 0 fail**.

**The 🔴 from round 1 is closed, at both seams.**

- **Route table.** `Route.audience` is a *required* field (`src/http/types.ts`), so a new route cannot be added without declaring a side; all 12 routes carry one (9 requisition + 1 rule = `member`, 2 outbox = `merchant`). `audienceGuard` runs in `handle` after `authenticate` and **before** `parseBody` and before `runMutating` spends an `Idempotency-Key` — a merchant token cannot even burn a key on a route it may not call, and body-shape errors cannot be used to probe a route it may not reach.
- **`isMember` excludes `merchant`.** `HUMAN_ROLES` is the four human roles; `merchant` is not among them. The `system` escape is sound: `resolveScope` only ever builds `kind: 'user'`, so no request can present a `system` actor — I checked the one construction path.
- **Service seam.** `detail`/`list`/`ruleTable` each call `memberGuard` first; `ruleTable`'s return type went to `Result<…>` and the route now forwards the refusal instead of wrapping it in a 200 — the seam is real, not a comment.

The remaining `ruleId`/`ruleCode` uses in `src/app/outbox.ts` are the internal `transition` and the audit line, not merchant-facing output — the feed serves only `payload_json`. The outbox is introduced in this same PR, so there are no version-1 rows left in any database to replay.
